chunks: "I'd group them by what property of the diode you're using. The obvious one is one-way conduction.

That gives you rectifiers, like a bridge turning AC into DC; reverse-polarity protection, where a series diode blocks current if someone plugs the battery in backwards; diode OR-ing, where two supplies feed one rail and whichever is higher wins; and flyback diodes across relay coils or motors, which give the inductor current somewhere to go when the transistor turns off so you don't get a huge voltage spike.
Second, you can use the reverse breakdown region on purpose. A Zener diode gives you a simple voltage reference or clamp, and a TVS diode absorbs ESD and surge on connectors.
Every IC pin also has little ESD diodes to the rails.

Third, the junction itself can be the point: LEDs emit light, photodiodes detect it, varactors are voltage-controlled capacitors for tuning, and the forward voltage's minus 2 millivolt per degree tempco is used as a temperature sensor.
The main trade-off is the forward drop.
A silicon diode in series with a 2 amp load burns over a watt, so for power paths I'd use a Schottky, or an ideal-diode MOSFET controller if efficiency really matters."
